title: Verifier‑Grounded Evaluation of LLM‑Generated Network Configurations (Estimand: verifier‑consistency under identical inputs)
abstract: We present a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1) that uses a deterministic network validator to compare a deterministic template baseline against a single‑pass LLM generator (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini) on N = 120 synthetic intent→configuration tasks. Preregistered confirmatory semantics reused a single canonical candidate per task across both scoring conditions (shared_initial_candidate). Under those frozen semantics all confirmatory episodes completed: baseline = 120/120 verifier passes; guarded (gpt‑5‑mini, shared seed) = 120/120 verifier passes. Paired difference = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We (1) publish the complete execution and analysis artifact bundle and SHA‑256 fingerprints required for byte‑for‑byte reproduction, (2) diagnose—using the archived traces—why the preregistered shared_initial_candidate design produces a degenerate paired result that does not measure independent generative reliability, and (3) provide artifact‑grounded, runnable modifications (independent_per_condition sampling, multi‑seed confirmatory design, validator diversification, and expanded task heterogeneity) that preserve reproducibility while answering the operational question practitioners typically require.

sections.introduction: Modern NetOps requires correct, auditable network configuration changes: transient misordering or malformed commands can break reachability, violate access lists, or create unsafe transient states during multi‑step changes. Deterministic offline validators (reachability/ACL/routing analyzers) are widely used operational oracles to check configuration artifacts before deployment [https://doi.org/10.1145/3603269.3604866]. Large language models (LLMs) promise fluent intent→configuration synthesis, but their stochasticity raises reliability and safety questions. We preregistered CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1 to evaluate a precise estimand: verifier‑consistency under identical inputs—i.e., whether a deterministic validator reports different pass/fail outcomes when presented with the same canonical candidate under two scoring conditions. This paper (i) releases the exact, hashed execution artifacts required for deterministic reproduction, (ii) reports the preregistered confirmatory outcome and corresponding exact analysis artifacts, and (iii) uses the archived evidence to explain why the preregistered design produces a degenerate paired contrast and how to rerun informative independent comparisons without losing reproducibility.
sections.related_work: Verifier grounding and generate–validate–repair workflows are established patterns for operationally meaningful NetOps automation: Batfish‑class analyzers compute forwarding/reachability and detect ACL/routing violations from static configurations [Brown et al., 2023; doi:10.1145/3603269.3604866]. Recent LLM→NetOps work varies on sampling semantics (single canonical vs independent per‑condition), repair budgets (single pass vs bounded iterative repair), and validator scope (syntactic vs semantic/behavioral checks). Studies that adopt independent sampling or multi‑seed replication directly estimate generative reliability; others that reuse single candidates measure validator determinism or repair efficacy. We position our artifact publication and preregistration as a complementary contribution emphasizing reproducibility and design diagnostics rather than a broad multi‑model benchmark. Representative nearest work includes recent intent→configuration evaluations and template‑based studies that highlight the sensitivity of measured pass rates to task synthesis and sampling choices [CN S M 2024; NEM 2025].
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen plan. The study preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1) was frozen before any model outputs (preregistration SHA‑256 7db1663cf3982c8ea1e16c3dd7c0348f356bb4cbe3978ecc75bb59fdedb71a37). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, confirmatory design: paired (N = 120 tasks), per‑pair shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (a single canonical LLM candidate produced once per task and reused for both scoring episodes), validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5, scoring rule = full_intent_constraint_validation, analysis executor = paired_binary_analysis_v1 with 10,000 bootstrap resamples (seed = 1729). Task synthesis. Tasks were programmatically generated from a deterministic template bank (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). Each task manifest encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, explicit required_sequence, workflow_policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, minimum_active_in_groups), allowed_touched_fields, and difficulty annotations. Representative task manifests and canonical candidates are archived under execution/task_manifest.jsonl and execution/responses/*.txt; example canonical candidate files include execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 8f38c8becd7e1e36...), execution/responses/task-000002-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 ae967f70dfb6ccb8...), and execution/responses/task-000003-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 f7f4db249ecbbce...). Model and orchestration. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini; adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1; execution/model_configuration.json archived (SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da...). Shared_initial semantics and model‑call accounting: to enforce the shared_initial_candidate estimand we produced one canonical generation per task and reused it for both baseline and guarded scoring episodes. As a result model_calls_used = 120 (counted once per canonical generation); planned maximum_model_calls = 240 (execution/execution_manifest.json lists the per‑file SHA‑256 manifest). Deterministic validator. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0) performs parsing, normalization, per‑task workflow policy enforcement, transient safety checks (e.g., minimum_active_in_groups) and final_state assertions. Each scoring episode emits a JSON validator trace archived under execution/scoring/*.json (representative: execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 0d56c1add7c5a57f...). Scoring rule. full_intent_constraint_validation is a binary pass (VALID_CONFIGURATION = 1) only if all required_sequence steps and transient constraints are honored and final_state matches the expected constraints. Execution accounting and retries. Planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 120. Preregistered retry policy permitted up to 2 automated retries for infrastructure failures; none were required. Contamination heuristics (exact match and normalized n‑gram overlap) were run per preregistration; results are recorded in analysis/contamination_summary.csv (artifact included). All provider call traces and call_cache artifacts are published to enable independent exposure analysis (execution/provider_calls/* and execution/call_cache/*).
sections.results: Confirmatory counts and deterministic artifacts. Under the frozen confirmatory semantics (shared_initial_candidate) every pair yielded identical canonical inputs for baseline and guarded scoring. The observed confirmatory counts are: complete_pair_count = 120, baseline_success_count = 120/120, guarded_success_count = 120/120. The paired contingency table is degenerate: n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 9f25790c7eeaafb3...). Statistical inference (preregistered). The paired estimator (mean of guarded_i − baseline_i) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All analysis artifacts (condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 9c77c96f37c4b6ff..., paired_difference_figure.svg SHA‑256 ae5b8e0c644f8cf7...) are archived and match these values. Representative validator traces. Each scoring JSON includes parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, transient enforcement results, and final_state. Example: execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (SHA‑256 0d56c1add7c5a57f...) shows parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, and validation_after.valid = true; the canonical candidate is execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 8f38c8becd7e1e36...). Deterministic causal chain. The execution and scoring artifacts make the causal chain explicit: an identical canonical candidate per pair fed a deterministic validator necessarily produces identical pass/fail outputs—hence the degenerate contingency. The artifacts required for byte‑for‑byte reproduction and independent audit are included in execution/execution_manifest.json (full per‑file SHA‑256 manifest).
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and estimand clarity. The confirmatory outcome correctly answers the preregistered estimand—validator response consistency to identical inputs—because the design intentionally reused canonical candidates per pair. It does not, however, estimate independent generative reliability: the probability that independently sampled LLM outputs (different seeds or independent per‑condition draws) pass the validator in deployment‑like conditions. Table mapping (operational question vs tested estimand). We provide a concise operational mapping (paper body and artifacts):

- Operational question practitioners usually need: "What is P[LLM candidate passes validator] when the LLM is sampled independently at runtime?" — requires independent_per_condition sampling and multi‑seed replication (NOT measured here).
- Preregistered estimand we tested: "Does a deterministic validator give different pass/fail outcomes when presented with the same canonical candidate under two scoring conditions?" — tested here via shared_initial_candidate; result: no difference (paired difference = 0.00).
- Why the difference matters: identical inputs plus deterministic scoring collapse paired contrasts and do not reveal LLM sampling variance or seed sensitivity.

Runnable, artifact‑grounded modifications. Using the archived pipeline one can deterministically run informative reruns without creating new tasks: (A) independent_per_condition confirmatory rerun — generate separate seed per condition per task (baseline seed_0, guarded seed_1), rescore with deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and compute paired contrasts; (B) multi‑seed confirmatory design — draw K ≥ 3 independent seeds per condition per task and estimate per‑condition pass probabilities with bootstrap CIs; (C) validator diversification — add a second, independent verifier and report intersection/union pass rates to mitigate validator–task coupling. Exact artifacts required for those reruns are published: execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da...), execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/provider_calls/*.json, and execution/scoring/*.json. Threats to validity (artifact‑identified). Internal validity: shared_initial semantics intentionally removed generation variance and thus precluded measuring independent generative reliability. Construct validity: template‑tight tasks with explicit required_sequences increase the chance that canonical, template‑aligned candidates satisfy deterministic validators. External validity: single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and synthetic tasks limit generalization to other models and open natural language intents. Conclusion validity: degenerate contingency tables yield trivial inferential outputs; interpreting them beyond the precise estimand is inappropriate. All threats are documented and visible in the archived traces.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired experiment and released the exhaustive artifact bundle (execution/execution_manifest.json and per‑file SHA‑256 fingerprints). Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics baseline and gpt‑5‑mini guarded both passed the deterministic validator on all N = 120 tasks. Archived validator traces demonstrate that identical canonical candidates per pair and template‑tight task constraints caused the degenerate paired outcome; therefore the confirmatory paired statistic does not estimate independent generative reliability. We provide precise, runnable, artifact‑grounded modifications (independent_per_condition sampling, multi‑seed replication, validator diversification, and expanded task heterogeneity) that preserve reproducibility while answering the operational reliability question NetOps practitioners require. All code, seeds, provider traces, scoring JSONs, and the immutable initial master prompt reference (provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) are included in the archive to support deterministic reruns and external audit.

limitations: Controlled synthetic tasks: programmatic templates produced narrow required_sequences and workflow_policies that favor canonical solutions and limit external generalizability to heterogeneous operational intents.

Confirmatory shared_initial semantics: the preregistered generation_semantics = 'shared_initial_candidate' supplied identical canonical candidates to both conditions per pair, removing generation variance and causing the degenerate paired outcome.
Single canonical seed for confirmatory test: the primary analysis used one canonical seed per task; preregistered exploratory multi‑seed analyses were not part of the reported confirmatory inference.

Validator–task coupling: the deterministic validator enforces constraints encoded in the task templates, which can increase pass rates for template‑aligned candidates and reduce construct validity for open distributions.

Possible training‑data exposure: preregistered contamination heuristics found no flags under chosen thresholds, but absence of a flag is not proof of zero exposure to related artifacts in model pretraining.

Single‑model, single‑validator run: results apply only to gpt‑5‑mini under the recorded configuration and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; they do not generalize across model families, agentic pipelines, or other validators.
